messages.content: I want to develop decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning that adapts to unfamiliar teammates without destabilizing coordination under partial observability. How should I state the goal precisely?

The goal is to enable agents to coordinate with unfamiliar teammates while each operates under partial observability and decentralized control. Adaptation matters, but it should not come at the expense of coordination with familiar teams. The two requirements make that balance concrete: achieve 20% higher normalized held-out teammate return than matched nonadaptive policies under identical observation constraints, and retain 95% of familiar-team return without teammate identities, communication, or test-time parameter sharing.
What does “under partial observability” add to the goal?

It means an agent cannot assume it has a complete view of the team or its environment when deciding how to act. The adaptation and coordination goals must hold with the information available to the agent, rather than depending on a full picture that the setting does not provide. That is also why the comparison with nonadaptive policies specifies identical observation constraints.
And why call the learning decentralized?

Decentralized describes the intended setting for the agents’ decisions: coordination cannot depend on a single decision-maker directing the whole team. In particular, the stated requirement rules out teammate identities, communication, and test-time parameter sharing as aids to meeting the familiar-team retention target. It does not, by itself, specify a particular learning algorithm or adaptation mechanism.
Can you unpack the unfamiliar-teammate requirement without assuming a specific mechanism?

An unfamiliar teammate is a teammate with whom the agent must still coordinate despite that lack of familiarity. The goal is for the agent’s behavior to adjust usefully in that situation. The node does not prescribe how it should make that adjustment, so it is better to describe adaptation as the desired capability, not as an implemented technique or an observed result.
I want the performance comparison to be unambiguous. What exactly is the 20% target comparing?

The target is 20% higher normalized held-out teammate return than matched nonadaptive policies. Both sides of that comparison must face identical observation constraints. “Held-out teammate” specifies the setting for the return being compared; “nonadaptive” specifies the kind of baseline. The statement does not further define the matching procedure or the normalization, so those details should not be filled in here.
Is 20% higher the same as an improvement of 20 percentage points?

No. The wording is “20% higher normalized held-out teammate return,” a relative comparison with the matched nonadaptive policies, not a claim of 20 percentage points. It also states a target to achieve, not a result that has already been measured.
Does the identical-observation condition apply only to the adaptive agent?

No. It is part of the comparison: the adaptive approach and the matched nonadaptive policies are to be assessed under identical observation constraints. That keeps the specified return advantage from being attributed simply to one side having access to more observations than the other.
How does the familiar-team requirement fit with adapting to held-out teammates?

It is the other side of the desired balance. Better return with held-out teammates is not enough if pursuing it undermines coordination with familiar teams. The requirement is to retain 95% of familiar-team return, while meeting the stated restrictions on teammate identities, communication, and test-time parameter sharing. The two targets therefore address different situations rather than substituting for one another.
When I say “without destabilizing coordination,” am I claiming there is a separate stability metric?

Not in the supplied goal. “Without destabilizing coordination” expresses what the adaptation should avoid, and retaining 95% of familiar-team return provides a concrete performance requirement relevant to that concern. No separate stability metric or threshold is specified, so it would be misleading to present one as part of the goal.
Should the absence of teammate identities be treated as the same thing as partial observability?

They are related constraints, but they are not interchangeable. Partial observability describes limited access to information more broadly. “Without teammate identities” specifically says the approach must not rely on knowing who a teammate is. The goal also separately excludes communication and test-time parameter sharing; none of those exclusions should be silently replaced by the broader phrase “partial observability.”
Does “without communication” mean agents cannot coordinate?

No. Coordination is the desired outcome; communication is one possible resource that the requirement says not to use. The challenge is precisely to adapt to unfamiliar teammates and preserve familiar-team performance without relying on communication, teammate identities, or test-time parameter sharing. That statement sets constraints, not a claim that coordination is impossible under them.
How would you put all of this into one concise objective without making it sound completed?

Develop decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning that adapts to unfamiliar teammates without destabilizing coordination under partial observability. Aim for 20% higher normalized held-out teammate return than matched nonadaptive policies under identical observation constraints, while retaining 95% of familiar-team return without teammate identities, communication, or test-time parameter sharing. This states the intended capability and its requirements without claiming they have already been achieved.
What approach could we propose for that objective without relying on teammate identities or communication?

One proposal is to train decentralized, local-history teammate-belief adapters using diverse training partners. Each adapter would confidence-gate residual actions on top of a frozen familiar-team policy. The proposal describes a way to attempt adaptation while keeping an existing familiar-team policy in place; it does not claim that either performance requirement has already been met.
Can you separate the parts of that proposal? There are several ideas packed into one sentence.

The familiar-team policy supplies the underlying behavior and remains frozen. A teammate-belief adapter uses the agent’s own local history to inform possible adjustments for the teammate it is encountering. Those adjustments take the form of residual actions layered on top of the frozen policy. A confidence gate controls the adapter’s contribution, and diverse training partners provide variation during training. The agents remain decentralized rather than depending on a shared decision-maker at test time.
What does “local-history” restrict the adapter to?

It means the adapter is based on what its own agent has locally observed over time, rather than requiring a complete, jointly observed account of the team. That fits the partial-observability setting. The proposal does not specify a particular history length, representation, or procedure for updating a belief, so those details remain open.
If it maintains a teammate belief, is that effectively a teammate identity in disguise?

Not necessarily. A teammate belief can mean an assessment formed from the local interaction history that helps the agent decide how to act; it need not be a known identity or an identity lookup. The distinction matters because the goal excludes teammate identities. The proposal should be understood as using local evidence about the interaction, not assuming access to an identity label.
Does the belief have to be a probability distribution over teammate types?

The proposal does not specify that. “Teammate-belief adapter” names the role of the adaptive component, but leaves its exact representation unspecified. Calling it a particular distribution, defining teammate types, or prescribing an inference procedure would add implementation choices that are not in the proposal.
Why put the adapter on top of a familiar-team policy instead of replacing that policy?

The proposed structure keeps familiar-team behavior available as a base while introducing a separate route for adaptation. Because the base policy is frozen, training the adapter does not itself mean retraining that base policy. This is a design rationale for the proposal, not a guarantee that familiar-team return will be retained at the required level.
What does “residual actions” mean here?

It indicates that the adapter contributes an adjustment relative to the frozen policy’s action, rather than serving as an entirely independent replacement policy. “Atop” expresses that relationship between the base behavior and the proposed adjustment. The proposal does not define an action-combination formula or specify how large an adjustment may be.
So does a frozen base policy mean the overall agent cannot change its behavior?

No. The base policy stays fixed, but the adapter’s residual contribution could change the action ultimately taken. Freezing the familiar-team policy and allowing adaptation through a separate component are compatible. Whether that combination preserves familiar-team performance is something the stated requirement would have to establish, not something freezing alone proves.
Explain the confidence gate without choosing a numerical threshold.

The gate makes the adapter’s influence conditional on confidence, rather than allowing every proposed residual to affect behavior equally. An intuitive motivation is to limit adjustments when the basis for them is uncertain, while permitting more influence when it is better supported. The proposal does not set a threshold, define how confidence is calculated, or establish that the confidence estimate is reliable.
Is the gate a guarantee that coordination will not be destabilized?

No. It is a proposed safeguard in the architecture, not a demonstrated guarantee. Residual actions could still be unhelpful, and a confidence gate could make poor judgments. The relevant question remains whether the complete approach adapts to unfamiliar teammates without destabilizing coordination and meets the specified return requirements.
What role do the diverse training partners play?

They provide variety for training the proposed adapters, so the adapter is not framed solely around one partner’s behavior. That is the extent of what the proposal says about them. It does not specify how partners are selected, how many there are, or what kinds of variation they exhibit, and it does not imply that training partners and held-out teammates are the same.
Does “decentralized” mean the adapters share their learned parameters with one another when facing a new team?

No. The approach is described as decentralized, and the goal rules out test-time parameter sharing. Each agent’s proposed adaptation is grounded in its own local history; it should not be described as relying on exchanging parameters during deployment. The proposal does not otherwise specify how any training-time components are organized.
Could the adapter ask the teammate for information to improve its belief?

That would not fit the stated goal’s no-communication condition. The proposal instead relies on local history for its teammate belief. This does not mean the agent has perfect knowledge of the teammate; it means the proposed adaptation must work with the information available without communication.
How does this proposal relate to the 20% improvement target?

The proposed adapter is intended to improve behavior with unfamiliar teammates. The quantitative target remains 20% higher normalized held-out teammate return than matched nonadaptive policies under identical observation constraints. Describing the architecture does not show that it achieves that comparison, and the proposal does not provide return measurements.
And the 95% familiar-team requirement?

The frozen familiar-team policy and confidence-gated residual actions are proposed in part to make adaptation compatible with preserving familiar-team coordination. The requirement is still to retain 95% of familiar-team return without teammate identities, communication, or test-time parameter sharing. Nothing in the proposal alone establishes that the retention level will be reached.
Would it be accurate to call the frozen policy the matched nonadaptive baseline?

Not on the information given. The frozen familiar-team policy is a component of the proposed adaptive approach, whereas “matched nonadaptive policies” identifies the comparison required for held-out teammate return. The proposal does not say those are identical, so they should not be equated.
Give me a careful one-paragraph description of the proposal.

Train decentralized teammate-belief adapters from each agent’s local history using diverse training partners. Let the adapters contribute residual actions atop frozen familiar-team policies, with their contributions governed by a confidence gate. This proposes a way to adjust behavior for unfamiliar teammates while retaining a familiar-team base under partial observability, without relying on teammate identities, communication, or test-time parameter sharing. It specifies an approach to the goal, not an observed improvement or a guarantee of familiar-team retention.
The question I want to isolate is this: can belief-confidence gating activate residual actions for unfamiliar partners while preserving frozen-policy behavior with familiar partners?

That is the central question for the proposed gate. It asks for selective adaptation, not simply whether an adapter can change actions. With unfamiliar partners, the gate would need to allow useful residual contributions when the local-history teammate belief supports them. With familiar partners, it would need to keep those contributions from disrupting the behavior supplied by the frozen policy. Neither outcome follows automatically from having a confidence gate.
Wouldn’t an unfamiliar partner make the adapter less confident, though?

It could. Unfamiliarity and confidence are not opposites with a fixed relationship: an agent might lack a basis for an adjustment, or its local history might eventually support one despite the partner being unfamiliar. The question therefore should not be read as asking the gate to switch on merely because a partner is unfamiliar. It asks whether confidence in the belief can govern residual actions in a way that permits adaptation when warranted.
So the confidence is about whether an adjustment is justified, not just whether the teammate seems familiar?

That is a useful distinction. If the gate treated confidence as nothing more than a familiarity signal, it would not by itself explain why an unfamiliar-partner residual should activate. The question is whether belief confidence can support the relevant decision about the residual’s contribution while also leaving frozen-policy behavior intact with familiar partners. It does not specify how that confidence is represented or assessed.
What counts as preserving frozen-policy behavior? Does the policy being frozen already do that?

Freezing the policy means its own parameters are not changed by the adapter. It does not mean the combined agent always acts as that policy would, because a residual action can alter the resulting behavior. Preserving frozen-policy behavior with familiar partners is therefore a separate part of the question: whether the gate can limit the residual’s influence appropriately in that situation.
If the residual contributes nothing, is the familiar-policy behavior preserved?

In the basic sense of a residual being an added adjustment, no residual contribution would leave the frozen policy to supply the action. But that observation does not establish the broader outcome in the question. The gate would have to behave appropriately across familiar-partner interactions, and the question does not assert that it does.
Is the intended behavior simply ‘gate off for familiar, gate on for unfamiliar’?

That is an intuitive shorthand, but it is too absolute for the question as worded. It asks whether belief-confidence gating can activate residual actions for unfamiliar partners while preserving frozen-policy behavior with familiar partners. It does not say every unfamiliar encounter must activate a residual, or that the gate has a direct familiar-versus-unfamiliar label. Its proposed basis is the teammate belief and its confidence.
Why is it important to frame both parts together?

Because either part on its own misses the tension. A gate that never allows residual actions might protect the frozen policy’s behavior but provide no adaptation for unfamiliar partners. A gate that frequently allows adjustments might provide opportunities to adapt but risk changing behavior with familiar partners. The question is whether the same gating arrangement can support both aims.
Does a confident belief guarantee a useful residual action?

No. Confidence in a belief and the usefulness of a residual action are distinct. A belief can be confident yet mistaken, and an adjustment can be unhelpful even if it follows the belief. That is why the question remains open: confidence gating is a proposed way to regulate the adapter, not proof that activated residuals improve coordination.
How does local history matter to this particular question?

The proposed teammate belief draws on the agent’s local history. Under partial observability, that history is the basis available to the adapter for forming its belief and any associated confidence; it is not complete knowledge of the partner. The question asks whether a gate relying on that limited basis can make the needed distinction in its effect on actions.
Would preserving behavior with familiar partners require knowing their identities?

The question does not require an identity-based rule. The proposal is a local-history teammate-belief adapter, and the goal excludes teammate identities. The issue is whether the gate can avoid disruptive residual contributions during familiar-partner interactions without being told who the partner is. We should not assume that it succeeds simply because a partner is familiar.
Could I answer the question by pointing out that the base policy stays frozen?

Not completely. That establishes a property of the base policy, but the question concerns the behavior of the combined policy and adapter. You would still need to know whether residual actions are activated appropriately for unfamiliar partners and whether their influence leaves familiar-partner behavior preserved. A frozen base alone settles neither gating behavior.
What if the gate is cautious everywhere?

Then it might limit changes to frozen-policy behavior, but it could also prevent residual actions from contributing when an unfamiliar partner calls for adaptation. Caution alone is not the full answer. The question is about selective activation alongside preservation, rather than minimizing the adapter’s influence in all cases.
And what if it is permissive everywhere?

That could allow more residual contributions with unfamiliar partners, but it would not explain how frozen-policy behavior remains preserved with familiar partners. The key is whether belief-confidence gating differentiates when a contribution is appropriate, not merely whether it allows contributions at all.
Can we state the question without implying the gate already works?

Yes: “Can a decentralized, local-history teammate-belief adapter use confidence gating to activate residual actions when interacting with unfamiliar partners, while preserving the behavior of its frozen familiar-team policy when interacting with familiar partners?” That keeps both desired effects in view and presents them as an open question rather than an established result.
Does ‘preserving’ have to mean absolutely no changed action with a familiar partner?

The question does not define preservation at that level of precision. It identifies frozen-policy behavior with familiar partners as what should be preserved, but it does not specify an action-by-action equality rule or a tolerance for deviations. It is safest to retain the wording rather than silently turn it into a stricter or weaker criterion.
What is the most important uncertainty in the question?

Whether confidence derived from a local-history teammate belief can regulate residual influence well enough to serve two different situations: permit useful adaptation with unfamiliar partners and avoid disrupting frozen-policy behavior with familiar ones. The proposed structure makes that a plausible question to investigate, but its components alone do not answer it.

I want to turn that open question into a testable hypothesis: history-gated residuals at an unfamiliar-partner probability greater than 0.8 improve held-out normalized return by at least 20% over frozen policies while retaining at least 95% familiar return. Is that a faithful statement?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than a result. It predicts that history-gated residuals, using an unfamiliar-partner probability >0.8 as the gating condition, will yield held-out normalized return ≥20% higher than frozen policies while retaining ≥95% familiar return. Those outcomes are claims to test; the threshold and the proposed architecture do not establish them on their own.
Why does the probability have to be greater than 0.8 rather than at least 0.8?
The stated condition is strictly >0.8. A value of exactly 0.8 does not meet it. Rephrasing it as ≥0.8 would change the hypothesis, even though the numerical difference may look small.
Is the probability the same thing as general confidence in the teammate belief?

The hypothesis makes the gate more specific by referring to an unfamiliar-partner probability. That can be discussed as part of belief-confidence gating, but the hypothesis does not define how the probability is produced or establish that it is well calibrated. It is important to keep the actual condition—unfamiliar-partner probability >0.8—rather than replace it with an unspecified feeling of confidence.
Does exceeding 0.8 mean every residual action will improve coordination?

No. The threshold says when the history-gated residuals are proposed to come into play; it is not a guarantee that the underlying estimate is correct or that a particular residual action is beneficial. The performance and familiar-return claims concern the proposed approach’s outcomes, which remain hypothetical.
What does “history-gated” contribute to the wording?

It ties the gating of residual actions to the agent’s history, consistent with the local-history teammate-belief proposal. The word does not specify a history length, a model for turning history into the unfamiliar-partner probability, or an exact rule for combining residual and frozen-policy actions. Those would be additional design details.
Am I assuming access to the partner’s identity in order to calculate that probability?

No such access is stated. The proposed setting excludes teammate identities, and the hypothesis speaks of a history-gated unfamiliar-partner probability, not an identity label supplied to the agent. Whether a probability based on available local history can serve the intended purpose is part of what the hypothesis leaves to be tested.
Could I say that the gate identifies an unfamiliar partner with more than 80% accuracy?

That would add a different claim. A probability threshold >0.8 is a condition on the gate’s output; it does not imply more than 80% classification accuracy. The hypothesis makes claims about held-out normalized return and familiar return, not about an identification-accuracy metric.
Please clarify the held-out return prediction, including its baseline.

The prediction is that held-out normalized return improves by at least 20% over frozen policies. The baseline named here is frozen policies, and the improvement is a relative ≥20% comparison. The hypothesis does not supply measured returns, so it should not be phrased as an observed improvement.
Is that necessarily the same baseline as the matched nonadaptive policies in the broader goal?

The hypothesis specifically names frozen policies as its comparison. It does not state that frozen policies and matched nonadaptive policies are identical, so the two labels should not be treated as interchangeable without additional information.
What about the familiar-partner side of the hypothesis?

It predicts retention of ≥95% familiar return while the history-gated residuals are used. That is the part addressing the concern that adaptation might disrupt behavior with familiar partners. The hypothesis does not report that retention has occurred, nor does it define an additional action-by-action preservation criterion.
Does it specify what familiar return is measured relative to?

No explicit reference for the 95% retention calculation is given in this hypothesis. It is accurate to say “retaining ≥95% familiar return,” but naming a particular denominator or measurement procedure would add a detail that is not stated.
Could the approach satisfy only one of the two return conditions and still support this hypothesis?

No. The prediction joins them: held-out normalized return is ≥20% higher than frozen policies, and familiar return is retained at ≥95%. Demonstrating only the held-out improvement or only familiar-return retention would not establish the full hypothesis as written.
If the probability never exceeds 0.8 with an unfamiliar partner, would the threshold alone solve the adaptation problem?

No. The threshold by itself cannot ensure residuals become active when useful. The hypothesis depends on the history-based probability and the resulting residual behavior working together to produce the stated return outcomes. It does not assert how often the threshold is crossed or how reliably that happens with unfamiliar partners.
Conversely, what if it exceeds 0.8 during an interaction with a familiar partner?

That illustrates why familiar-return retention is a substantive part of the hypothesis. The probability might not perfectly distinguish situations, and residual actions could then affect familiar-partner behavior. The ≥95% familiar-return prediction must stand or fall with the overall behavior; it cannot be inferred merely from having the >0.8 gate.
Should we describe the residuals as replacing the frozen policy when they activate?

No. The proposal places residual actions atop frozen familiar-team policies. Describing them as replacing the frozen policy would change the relationship between the components. The hypothesis concerns whether gating those residual contributions produces the two stated return outcomes.
Give me a final version that makes the uncertainty explicit but keeps every number and comparison.

Hypothesis: History-gated residual actions activated at an unfamiliar-partner probability >0.8 will improve held-out normalized return by ≥20% over frozen policies while retaining ≥95% familiar return. This is a prediction about both adaptation and preservation, not a report that either outcome has been achieved.
How should we investigate whether confidence gating lets the adapter act with unfamiliar partners without disturbing familiar-partner behavior?

The plan is to train history-only adapters, then sweep confidence thresholds around 0.8. Compare their behavior with frozen baselines on both held-out and familiar partners, using identity-free decentralized inference throughout. That puts both sides of the question in view: whether gating permits useful residual actions with held-out partners and whether it preserves behavior with familiar partners. It is a plan for investigation, not a result.
What does “history-only” require of the adapters?

Their adaptive input is the agent’s own interaction history, rather than a supplied teammate identity. That keeps the proposed adaptation grounded in information available locally. The plan does not specify how much history is retained or how it is represented.
Is that the same as saying inference is identity-free?

They are related but distinct parts of the plan. “History-only adapters” describes the information used by the adaptive component. “Identity-free decentralized inference” describes how the trained approach is to operate when it makes decisions: without teammate identity information and without a central decision-maker. Stating both makes the intended constraint explicit.
Why sweep thresholds instead of checking only 0.8?

A sweep asks how the gating behavior changes as the confidence threshold varies around 0.8. Checking only one threshold would not show whether the held-out and familiar-partner comparisons depend strongly on that particular setting. The plan does not prescribe the values in the sweep or identify a preferred threshold in advance.
Does “around 0.8” include thresholds both below and above it?

That is the natural reading of a sweep around 0.8: examine its neighborhood rather than treating 0.8 as the only setting. The plan does not state the range, spacing, or number of thresholds, so those should remain unspecified.
Should I say the sweep will find the optimal threshold?

Not yet. The plan calls for sweeping thresholds and making comparisons; it does not define an optimization criterion or claim that the sweep will identify an optimum. It would be more accurate to say the sweep will examine how the comparisons vary with the confidence threshold.
What exactly gets compared on the held-out partners?

The behavior of the trained, gated adapters at the swept thresholds is compared against frozen baselines with held-out partners. This addresses the adaptation side of the question. The plan does not report the comparison’s outcome or give a detailed measurement procedure.
And why include familiar partners in the same plan?

Because an adapter could affect interactions with familiar partners even if it is intended to help with unfamiliar ones. Comparing against frozen baselines on familiar partners lets the investigation consider whether gating leaves the familiar-policy behavior intact, rather than examining adaptation alone. The plan does not presume that preservation will occur.
Are the held-out and familiar comparisons separate tests?

They are two settings in the stated evaluation: held-out partners and familiar partners. Considering both is essential to the question being investigated. The plan does not specify how partners are grouped, how many are used, or any further testing protocol.
Does “held-out” mean those partners are used to train the history-only adapters?

No. Calling partners held-out distinguishes them from the adapters’ training interactions. The plan is to train the adapters and examine the threshold sweep with held-out as well as familiar partners; it should not be paraphrased as training on the held-out partners. The exact separation procedure is not specified.
Would it be fair to describe the frozen baseline as a policy with no adaptive residual contribution?

That captures the comparison at a general level: the frozen baselines provide a nonadjusting reference against which to examine the adapters’ gated behavior. But the plan does not specify an exact baseline construction, so I would avoid adding details about how its actions are computed or asserting that it is identical to a particular component of the adapter.
Can the threshold sweep by itself show that the gate is selecting unfamiliar partners correctly?

Not by itself. The sweep can expose how changing the confidence condition relates to the held-out and familiar-partner comparisons. It does not automatically establish that the underlying confidence estimates correctly distinguish partners, or that every activated residual is appropriate. Those would be stronger conclusions than the plan states.
Could I call it an identity-recognition test?

That would mischaracterize it. Inference is explicitly identity-free. The plan investigates confidence-gated adaptation using local history, including its effects with held-out and familiar partners; it does not require the agent to recognize or be given a teammate’s identity.
What does decentralized inference rule out in the way we describe the comparison?

It rules out describing test-time decisions as dependent on a central controller that combines the agents’ information to choose their actions. The comparisons are to be made with agents operating under decentralized inference. The plan does not provide further implementation details about that inference.
If a threshold looks good with held-out partners, can we stop there?

That would leave the other half of the question unanswered. The plan explicitly includes comparisons with familiar partners against frozen baselines. A held-out-partner comparison alone would not tell us whether the gated residuals preserve familiar-partner behavior.
Could the familiar-partner comparison alone answer the question?

No. Staying close to a frozen baseline with familiar partners would address preservation, but not whether residual actions contribute usefully with held-out partners. The reason to examine both settings across the threshold sweep is that the question asks for adaptation and preservation together.
Is the plan claiming that a threshold near 0.8 will balance those two aims?

No. Around 0.8 is the region the plan proposes to examine, not a demonstrated balance point. The held-out and familiar comparisons are needed precisely because the effect of changing the confidence threshold is not established here.
How much should we say about training the adapters?

Say that the adapters will be trained to use local history and that their confidence-gated behavior will then be examined. The plan does not give a training algorithm, a training duration, or a detailed account of the training partners. Adding those as settled choices would go beyond it.
Does this plan determine how confidence is calculated?

No. It presupposes confidence thresholds that can be swept, but it does not specify the confidence calculation. The earlier question concerns belief-confidence gating, while this plan states what will be trained and compared. Neither the representation of confidence nor its reliability is established by the plan.
Can you phrase the plan without suggesting the experiment has already been run?

Train history-only adapters, then sweep confidence thresholds around 0.8 and compare the gated approach against frozen baselines with held-out and familiar partners under identity-free decentralized inference. The comparisons are intended to investigate whether residual actions can be activated for unfamiliar partners while frozen-policy behavior is preserved with familiar partners; their outcomes remain open.
What is the concrete activity for the gate sweep?

Run gate sweeps over 0.6–0.9 on PartnerShift-PO, comparing held-out normalized return and familiar retention against frozen policies across 10 seeds. That specifies the setting, the threshold range, the two comparisons, and the number of seeds. It does not report an outcome.
What exactly is being swept?
The gate threshold is being varied across the 0.6–0.9 range. The activity does not specify the increments, the number of threshold settings, or a rule for choosing one setting after the comparisons.
Does that range let us look on both sides of 0.8?
Yes. The stated range extends below and above 0.8, so it can examine how the comparisons vary around that value. That does not imply that any threshold in the range will perform better than another.
Should I say every value between 0.6 and 0.9 will be tested?
No. A sweep over 0.6–0.9 identifies a range, not every possible value within it. The activity leaves the threshold spacing unspecified.
What can we safely say about PartnerShift-PO?
It is the named setting for this activity. The node does not describe its tasks, observations, partners, or scoring procedure, so those details should not be inferred from the name.
Are we comparing held-out return with familiar retention directly?

No. They are two things to compare against frozen policies: held-out normalized return and familiar retention. The activity calls for examining both, not treating them as the same metric or subtracting one from the other.
Why keep the frozen policies in both comparisons?

They are the reference named in the activity for assessing both held-out normalized return and familiar retention. Using that reference makes it possible to ask how gated behavior compares in each setting. The activity does not say what those comparisons will show.
Can I call the frozen policies matched nonadaptive policies?

The activity calls them frozen policies. It does not establish that they are identical to any separately described set of matched nonadaptive policies, so keeping the stated name avoids adding a baseline equivalence.
What does ‘across 10 seeds’ commit us to?

It specifies 10 seeds for the activity. It does not say there are 10 partners, 10 threshold values, or 10 observations per threshold. Nor does it provide results from those seeds or specify how they will be summarized.
Does the seed count prove a result would be reliable?
No. Ten seeds describe the scope of the runs, not the strength or consistency of any outcome. The activity contains no seed-level returns, variation estimates, or conclusions.
How does this activity bear on the proposed >0.8 gating hypothesis?

The 0.6–0.9 sweep includes thresholds in the neighborhood of 0.8 and extends above it. Comparing held-out normalized return and familiar retention against frozen policies can therefore inform the prediction about gating near that condition. The activity itself does not establish the predicted return improvement or retention.
Is a gate threshold of 0.8 the same statement as an unfamiliar-partner probability greater than 0.8?

They should not be collapsed into one claim. One describes a threshold setting in the sweep; the other describes a strict activation condition on a probability. The activity does not specify the gate’s exact inequality at each swept setting, so it would be premature to assert how a value exactly equal to a threshold is handled.
Could the sweep establish that residual actions activate only for unfamiliar partners?

Not from the activity description alone. It calls for return and retention comparisons over gate thresholds. It does not report which actions activate in particular interactions or claim that the gate perfectly distinguishes unfamiliar from familiar partners.
What if held-out normalized return improves but familiar retention falls?

That would illustrate why the activity compares both quantities. A change in held-out normalized return alone would not answer what happened to familiar retention. But that is a hypothetical reading of possible comparisons, not a reported outcome of the 10-seed sweep.
And if familiar retention is strong but held-out return does not improve?

That would likewise speak to only one side of the intended balance. The activity is set up to compare both held-out normalized return and familiar retention against frozen policies, without presuming that either comparison will be favorable.
Is it accurate to write that we found the best gate setting on PartnerShift-PO?

No. The node directs a sweep; it gives no results and does not define a criterion for a ‘best’ setting. A faithful description says the thresholds will be swept over 0.6–0.9 and the two comparisons will be made across 10 seeds.
Give me a compact activity statement with no implied findings.

Run 0.6–0.9 gate sweeps on PartnerShift-PO across 10 seeds, comparing held-out normalized return and familiar retention against frozen policies. The comparisons are to be performed; no result or selected threshold is stated.
What did the PartnerShift-PO gate sweep show at 0.8?

On PartnerShift-PO, gating at 0.8 raised held-out normalized return from 0.50 to 0.62 and retained 97% of the familiar baseline across 10 seeds. Those are the reported figures for that gate setting; no results for other thresholds are given here.
How large is the held-out return change in absolute terms?
It is an increase of 0.12 in normalized return: 0.62 minus 0.50. That is an absolute difference on the reported normalized-return scale, not a change of 0.12 in familiar retention.
